items.prose: You buy £5,000,000 of past winners and pay for them by selling £5,000,000 of past losers short.
items.question: How much of your own capital do the trades need, before margin and fees?

options.why: You counted the purchase but not the cash the short sale raises.
That is the gross exposure, the two legs added, not capital.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the cash the two trades use and raise.

explain.text: The short sale raises the £5,000,000 that buys the winners. That is why a momentum paper reports a spread rather than a return on capital.

items.prose: You want to know whether a paper's sample keeps shares that later delisted.
items.question: Which section answers that?

options.why: An abstract rarely has room for the treatment of delisted shares.
The table shows results, not how the sample was built.
The introduction argues why the result matters.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Which section says how the sample was built?

explain.text: Universe, dates, source and the treatment of delisted shares all belong in the data section. That is why it is read second, straight after the abstract.

items.prose: A 12/9 strategy, well inside the sample, no skip.
items.question: How many cohorts are live in month 100?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the cohorts still in their holding period.

byKey.j: You used J. Each cohort is held K = 9 months, so 9 are live.

explain.text: Cohorts ranked in months 92 to 100 are live in month 100: nine of them, one per holding month. J only sets how far back each ranking looks.

items.prose: J = 6, K = 3, skip 1. A cohort is ranked at the start of month 50.
items.question: What is the first month of its ranking window?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Leave out month 49, then count six months back.

byKey.noskip: Month 44 starts the window with no skip. With skip 1 it ends at 48, so it starts at 43.
byKey.seven: Month 42 gives a seven-month window. J = 6.

explain.text: The skip leaves out month 49, so the window ends at month 48. Six months ending at 48 start at 43. Holding still starts in month 50.

items.prose: A J/K cell shows a spread of 0.77% a month.
items.question: What is that compounded over a year, in %?

explain.text: $(1.0077)^{12} - 1 = 0.0964$. Simple multiplication gives 9.24%, which leaves out the return on earlier gains.

items.prose: Our 12/12 cell: mean 0.66% a month, sd 6.21%, 277 months.
items.question: What is its t statistic, to 2 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the mean by sd / √n.

byKey.sd: You divided by the sd. Divide it by √277 first.

explain.text: √277 = 16.64, so the standard error is 6.21 / 16.64 = 0.373 and t = 0.66 / 0.373 = 1.77. That is short of 1.96 despite a sizeable mean.

items.prose: A replication on free data gets 0.70% a month for 12/3, with standard error 0.30%. The paper reports about 1.31%.
items.question: How many standard errors apart are they, to 2 decimal places?

feedback.correct: Correct. 2.03, just outside a two standard error rule.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the gap by the standard error.

byKey.raw: That is the gap in % a month. Divide it by the 0.30% standard error.

explain.text: 0.61 / 0.30 = 2.03, just beyond k = 2. Under the rule fixed in advance it is not a match. The note reports it with its likely cause, rather than moving k.

items.prose: A made-up log from a replication run.

lines: ranking window for month 120: months 114 to 119
params.title: Terminal

items.question: Tap the line that fails its check.

feedback.correct: Correct. The weights sum to 0.11 and gross 2.11.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare each line with what a correct step must show.

byKey.l2: Months 114 to 119 end at t − 1 for month 120. That window is right.
byKey.l3: Ten deciles of 50 sum to 500. That check passes.
byKey.l5: A placebo near 0 is what working code shows.

explain.text: Weights must sum to 0 and gross to 2. Winners at +1/45 against losers at −1/50 give a net long book: 50/45 − 1 = 0.11. The placebo barely notices, which is why each step has its own check.

items.prose: A colleague's code finds a 6/1 spread of 17% a month on the seeded panel and 18% on a shuffled copy.
items.question: What should they conclude?

options.text: The code creates the spread, most likely by looking ahead

options.why: You read the spread's size as evidence. The shuffled copy has no momentum, yet the code finds 18% there.
Noise does not give 17% a month twice. Something in the code produces it.
Working code would find about 0 on a shuffled copy. The fault is in the code.

feedback.correct: Correct. A spread on shuffled data comes from the code.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what the shuffled copy can contain.

explain.text: A shuffled panel has no link between past and future, so any spread there comes from the code. The usual cause is a ranking window that includes the traded month. Check the formation step first.
